messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 29
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Jeweler
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Somatic (Heart Racing): Own heart racing or pounding, Auditory (Children Crying): Kids crying, Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
  Maladaptive Strategies: Downward Comparison: I remind myself it could have been worse, Positive Reframing: I force myself to think only positive thoughts, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things

Vignette:
Caleb Merritt is a 29-year-old single man who works as a jeweler in a small independent shop in Portland, Oregon. He presented for psychological assessment approximately eight months after returning from a fourteen-month deployment with an international humanitarian relief organization operating in a conflict zone in the Middle East. His PCL-5 score of 70 places him in the severe range of post-traumatic stress, and the picture that emerged across his intake and early sessions is one of a young man who has returned to the physical landscape of his former life while remaining, in almost every meaningful sense, somewhere else entirely.

Caleb had volunteered with the relief organization in his mid-twenties, motivated by what he described as a need to do something that mattered. He was assigned to a field clinic in a region where shelling was intermittent and unpredictable, and his role involved coordinating supply distribution and, when the medical staff were overwhelmed, providing basic triage support. The incident that he identifies as the organizing center of his current suffering occurred during a mortar strike on a residential area adjacent to the clinic. In the immediate aftermath, Caleb was among the first to enter the site. He worked for hours alongside medical personnel in conditions of extreme chaos. What he cannot move past — what he returns to without choosing to — is the specific texture of that afternoon: the sound of children crying out beneath rubble, the press of hands grabbing at him as he moved through the crowd, and the physical sensation in his own chest as adrenaline pushed his heart into a pounding that he thought, in those moments, might itself kill him. He survived. Many did not. He flew home fourteen months later carrying, he said, a weight he had no name for.

In the months following his return, Caleb noticed that the world around him had developed edges he had never perceived before. At the jewelry shop where he had worked before his deployment, he found himself cataloguing the room each morning before unlocking the cases — noting the letter opener on the counter, the heavy loupe on its stand, the small engraving tools arranged in a row. He was certain, in a way he could not argue himself out of, that he needed to know where every potentially dangerous object was at all times. He repositioned his workbench so that his back was against the rear wall, telling his employer it helped with the lighting. When a customer came up behind him without warning and placed a hand on his shoulder to get his attention, Caleb's body responded before his mind could intervene — he spun, knocked a tray of rings to the floor, and stood breathing hard while the customer apologized, bewildered. Caleb apologized too, and spent the rest of the afternoon convinced that something fundamental was broken in him.

He had developed private strategies to manage what he was experiencing. When the memories pressed in, he reminded himself that others had suffered far worse — that he, at least, had come home. He made deliberate efforts to redirect his thinking toward positive images, toward plans, toward anything that was not the inside of that afternoon. These efforts cost him enormous energy and, he admitted, rarely held for long. The memories arrived not always as images but sometimes as pure emotional weather — a wave of dread or grief with no picture attached to it, only the full weight of the feeling, which he found in some ways more frightening than the explicit recollections. When a child cried in the street outside the shop, or when his own pulse quickened after carrying a heavy delivery up the stairs, the afternoon could return with a completeness that ordinary memories never possessed. He had come to believe that his memories of the event were simply more real than anything else in his life, and he was not sure whether that terrified him or confirmed something he already suspected about what he had witnessed.

What finally brought Caleb to seek help was a conversation with his younger sister, who told him quietly that she felt she had lost him — that he had come back from overseas but had not really come home. He could not disagree. What he hopes for, cautiously, is to stop scanning every room he enters. What he fears most is that the clinician will tell him he is safe, and that he will be entirely unable to believe it.
